analysis.one_liner: Sets federal rules limiting how Medicare Advantage plans use prior authorization and deny claims.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in September 2026 and sent to two House committees, where no action has been taken with the session ending in early January.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare Advantage is the private-insurer version of Medicare, covering more than half of Medicare beneficiaries. These plans require doctors to get advance approval ('prior authorization') before many treatments and services, and they deny claims after care is delivered; patients and doctors then go through appeals that can delay or cancel needed care. The bill would write federal requirements into Medicare law to rein in how often these plans use prior authorization and how they handle denials, including reporting requirements. It was introduced late in the session and referred to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees, which oversee Medicare, and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare Advantage enrollees who face delays or denials of care, plus the doctors and hospitals that spend staff time fighting prior authorization requests and appeals. Seniors in plans with high denial rates would get clearer federal protections and more visibility into insurer denial practices.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare Advantage enrollees and their doctors

how_it_helps.text: The bill establishes requirements for how Medicare Advantage plans use prior authorization and handle claims denials under Medicare law [S1].
Referral to both Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce is consistent with the bill covering Medicare payment and oversight provisions that fall under both committees' jurisdiction [S1].

analysis.who_pays: Medicare Advantage insurers, who profit partly by holding down spending through prior authorization and claims denials. Tighter federal rules would reduce that tool, and insurers argue it could raise plan costs and premiums. Taxpayers could see higher Medicare Advantage program costs if utilization rises.

drawbacks.text: Insurers and some policy analysts argue that prior authorization controls costs and prevents inappropriate care, and that limits on it could raise Medicare Advantage premiums or federal spending; the bill text provided does not detail the specific requirements, so its practical strength is hard to judge [S1].
With only one cosponsor and no committee action, the bill has no demonstrated path to becoming law in this session [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Reining in prior authorization addresses a well-documented pain point for seniors and their doctors. The trade-off is real but manageable in principle: utilization controls do restrain Medicare Advantage spending, so the design would matter a great deal. As written here, the bill is a statement of intent more than a working law, since it has never received a hearing or a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It has been sitting with the House Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees since mid-September with no hearing, markup, or floor vote scheduled, and only about three months remain in the session.

narrative.text: Rep. Greg Landsman introduced the bill on September 15, 2026 [S1].
It was referred to the Committee on Ways and Means and the Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S3].
One Republican House member cosponsored it [S2].
No further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — appears in the bill's action history [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, Medicare Advantage insurers are better off: with no committee movement, the current rules allowing broad prior authorization and claim denials remain untouched.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor's party are known, but with only two members attached there is not enough record to say how the parties would split if it ever came to a vote.

industries.note: These plans make money partly by managing utilization through prior authorization and claims denials; federal requirements in this area would cut into that practice. The bill would leave them in place as the delivery system for most Medicare beneficiaries while constraining how they manage care.
Providers spend substantial staff time submitting prior authorization requests and appealing denials; limits on the practice reduce that administrative burden and speed up patient care.

analysis.trajectory: With roughly three months left in the session, one cosponsor, and no hearing or markup scheduled in either committee, the bill is very likely to die at the end of this Congress without a vote. A new Congress would require reintroduction from scratch.
